The model predicts you have a 37% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you graduate.

The decision is driven mainly by three key aspects of your situation. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed three classes in the past. Among students who passed, the average number of previous failures is zero, so this history strongly pushes the model toward expecting you will fail again.

Two other factors pulled in the opposite direction. You did not attend nursery school, a background that the model associates with better long-term outcomes; this actually worked in your favor. Similarly, having only a low amount of free time after school also nudged the prediction slightly toward passing, as most successful students report medium or high free time.

Even with these helpful elements, your repeated past failures outweighed them. To improve, focus first on breaking the pattern of failing subjects. Speak with your teachers about targeted support in the areas where you struggled before, create a realistic study schedule that goes beyond your current two hours or less per week, and consider using the internet resources now available to you. Addressing the root causes of those earlier failures gives you the best chance of passing this year and avoiding further remedial obligations. (218 words)
